title: Being Explicit About Explicit Instruction
author: SoL in the Wild
summary: A teacher who has made explicit instruction the core of his practice argues that using a research-backed method is not enough: families need to understand what it is and why. He catalogues five misconceptions parents are likely to hold (that it is just telling answers, that students should struggle first, that it is rigid, that easy means something is wrong, and that it is boring) and answers each with cognitive load theory, Rosenshine and the evidence on minimal guidance. He then lists what he wants parents to understand: thinking depends on knowledge, explicit teaching supports equity, it models expert thinking, aims at transfer, and builds metacognition. A concrete communication plan follows, covering back-to-school materials, conferences, weekly newsletters and classroom artifacts. The piece is a practical model of translating evidence-informed teaching for a lay audience.
points: Explicit instruction attracts predictable parental misconceptions, and each can be answered with specific cognitive science (working memory limits, worked examples, Rosenshine's principles).
Students describing the approach as easy signals well-managed cognitive load, not low challenge.
The case for the method rests on knowledge as the base for critical thinking, equity for students with less prior knowledge, and long-term transfer.
Being evidence-informed includes explaining the method to families through a deliberate plan: course overviews, open house, newsletters, and notes on student work.
quotes: While explicit instruction is one of the most evidence-based ways to build knowledge and skills, it often comes with misconceptions that can create confusion or resistance among parents.

Research shows that minimally guided instruction is less effective, particularly for novice learners, because it overloads working memory and assumes background knowledge that many students don’t yet have. Explicit instruction does not prevent student inquiry and exploration; it enables it by ensuring students have the knowledge base to think critically and problem-solve later on.

Some students may describe explicit instruction as clear, straightforward, or even “easy” compared to more open-ended, minimally guided approaches. But this is not a sign of low challenge. It’s a sign that cognitive load is being managed effectively. Learning should be effortful, but not confusing.
In order to think deeply and more independently, students need something to think with. Knowledge isn’t the enemy of critical thinking, it’s the foundation.

Students arrive with different levels of background knowledge and support. Explicit instruction reduces the gap between students who have that prior knowledge and those who don’t. It doesn’t assume, it builds. It’s one of the most powerful ways to make instruction inclusive and responsive to diverse learners.

If I want parents to understand and support explicit instruction, I can’t assume they’ll “pick it up” from classroom materials or student work. Just as I teach students explicitly, I need to communicate explicitly with families about my instructional approach.

Sure, it’s not made for “Teacher Tik Tok”. It probably won’t win me any “Teacher of the Year” awards. But it works. And when parents understand the cognitive science behind it, they see that it’s not about doing less of this or more of that. It’s about teaching better.
